title: The task
subtitle: what the lander senses, does, and is scored on

transcript.text: Lesson one. The task. Before we evolve anything, let's look closely at the problem our pilot has to solve.

This is Lunar Lander, a small physics game from the Gymnasium library. The lander starts near the top of the screen with a random push, and it has to touch down softly on the pad between the two flags. Many times a second, the lander senses eight numbers. Its position, across and up. Its speed, across and up. Its tilt, and how fast it is spinning. And two switches that turn on when a leg touches the ground. With those eight numbers, it picks one of four actions. Do nothing. Fire the left engine. Fire the main engine underneath. Or fire the right engine. The side engines push the lander sideways and spin it, and the main engine pushes it up.

Every episode builds a new moon. The mountains are random, and the lander starts with a random shove, so no two flights are the same. The landing pad never moves, though. It's always in the middle, at the same height, and the lander's position inputs are measured from the pad. Zero, zero means right on target. During training, every pilot is tested on ten random moons, so evolution has to find a rule that works on all of them, instead of memorising one.

The game keeps score while it flies. Moving toward the pad, slowing down, and staying level all earn a little. Drifting away, speeding up, and tilting all cost a little. There are bigger events too. Each leg that touches the ground earns ten points. Coming to rest earns a hundred. Crashing costs a hundred. And fuel isn't free. Every frame the main engine fires costs a third of a point. The side engines cost a tenth as much. Add it all up over one flight. A score of two hundred or more counts as solved.
Lesson two. The controller. How can thirty-six numbers fly a spacecraft?

Our pilot is one small table of numbers, called a matrix. Each of the eight inputs is multiplied by four weights, one for each action. Then a bias is added to each total. That gives four scores. Whichever score is highest, that action fires. Watch the scores on the right change as the lander flies, and the winning action change with them. Eight inputs times four actions is thirty-two weights. Add four biases, and you have thirty-six numbers. That is the entire pilot.

Let's learn to read the table. Each row is one input, and each column is one action. Orange cells are positive weights, and blue cells are negative. The brighter the cell, the bigger the number. Read across a row, and you see how one input votes. The tilt pushes some actions up and others down, all at the same time. Read down a column, and you see everything that argues for one action. This is the right engine's column. A single cell is a single rule. A positive weight means the bigger this input, the more I want this action. A negative weight means the opposite. Here: tilting left is a strong vote for the right engine, which turns the lander back upright. The last row is the bias. It's a head start, or a handicap, that each action gets, whatever the state.

Now let's watch one real decision. Each input is multiplied by its weight, and the products are added up in each column. The lander is falling fast, so the falling speed pushes the main engine's score up. It has the highest total, just barely, so the main engine fires.

title: Population and fitness
subtitle: many candidates, and a way to rank them

transcript.text: Lesson three. Population and fitness. Evolution needs two things. Many candidates, and a way to tell the good ones from the bad.

We start with a population of pilots. Each one is thirty-six random numbers. In training there are fifty of them. Here are eighteen. Each pilot flies, and we score it. With random numbers, every one of them crashes. But some crash later, or closer to the pad, and that difference is all evolution needs. We keep the best half, and the rest are thrown away. The survivors decide where the next generation will be sampled.

So what is the score? Each pilot flies ten different episodes, each with its own terrain and starting push. Then we combine three things. First, the average reward from the game itself. That already rewards approaching the pad, and it punishes crashing and wasted fuel. Second, a bonus of a hundred points, times the share of episodes that end in a landing. Landing is what we really want, so it's worth a lot. Third, a small speed bonus, up to thirty points, for landing quickly. It is multiplied by the landing rate, so a pilot can't earn it by crashing fast. Fourth, a penalty. Every frame an engine fires after both legs are on the ground costs half a point. Without it, evolution happily kept pulsing the side engines after touchdown, because they are almost free. With it, the pilot learns to land, and then stay still.

title: Inside CMA-ES
subtitle: how the search decides where to look next

transcript.text: Lesson four. Inside CMA-ES. How does the algorithm decide where to look next?
Every generation runs the same loop. Sample new pilots. Fly them. Rank them. Then update, and repeat. The algorithm never looks inside the pilot. It only sees the scores.

The new pilots are drawn from a cloud, a bell-shaped distribution over all thirty-six numbers. It has three parts. The mean is the centre of the cloud. It's the algorithm's current best guess for a good pilot. The step size, sigma, sets how far from the mean new candidates land. Big steps explore. Small steps fine-tune. And the covariance sets the shape. It lets the cloud stretch in the directions where good pilots were found, and stay narrow everywhere else. In our problem the cloud has thirty-six dimensions, one per weight. To watch it work, let's shrink it down to two.

Here is a toy problem with two numbers. Dark means low cost, which is good, and bright means high cost. The green cross is the best answer, but the algorithm doesn't know where it is. Each generation, it samples twelve points and keeps the best six, shown in orange. It moves the mean toward them, and reshapes the ellipse to follow the direction the winners came from. Watch the cloud stretch along the valley and race down it. As it closes in, the step size shrinks, until it settles on the answer. Learning that shape is what the name means: covariance matrix adaptation.
Lesson five. Generations. Now let's watch the population improve, one generation at a time.

Each dot is one pilot. Each column is one generation of fifty pilots, and the height of a dot is its fitness. Red pilots mostly crash, and green ones mostly land. In the first twenty generations, nearly every pilot crashes. But each generation is sampled around the best of the last one, so the whole column creeps upward. The best pilot lands half its episodes by generation twenty. Then the whole population climbs. By generation fifty, more than half the pilots land. By seventy-five, almost all of them do, and by one hundred, every single one. The orange line is the best pilot, and the blue line is the average. As the population agrees on one strategy, the average catches up with the best.

Fitness is just a number, so let's watch the flights. Every pilot of a generation starts from exactly the same spot, with the same push, and we draw where each one goes. Generation zero is chaos. Pilots fall straight down, or fire an engine and fly off the screen. One generation later, one pilot lands, almost by luck. By generation five, none do. At generation ten, still none. Then it takes off. Three pilots land at generation twenty, fourteen at thirty, twenty-seven at forty, and thirty-six at fifty. By seventy-five, forty-eight land. By the end, all fifty, and the trails bundle into one smooth curve down to the middle of the pad.

This is the same population, seen as points. Each pilot is thirty-six numbers. A method called principal component analysis flattens them down to two, so each dot is a whole pilot. The centre of the cloud, in blue, travels a long way from where it started, toward the region where pilots land. The white line is its path. Here is a neat trick. Only the highest score matters, so if you double every weight, every decision stays the same. The weights grew about a hundred times bigger, while the step size stayed around one. So each step got smaller and smaller compared with the weights, and the search turned into fine-tuning on its own.

title: Evolution in flight
subtitle: the best pilot along the way

transcript.text: Lesson six. Evolution in flight. What does the best pilot look like along the way?

Here is the best pilot from different points in training, all facing the same start. A random pilot, then the champions of generations ten, thirty, sixty and one hundred, and the final best. The random pilot fires its main engine without a break, and flies away. The champion of generation ten fires its engines, but still crashes. From generation thirty on, every champion lands.

Here is the centre of the population, drawn as the weight matrix itself. The colours are scaled to the biggest weight in each generation, so we can see the pattern while it forms. At generation zero it is noise. The strongest rules in the end are about tilt, spin and drift. Tilting left or spinning left fires the right engine. Drifting right fires the left engine. And the leg switches, which only matter at the very end, tell it to go quiet.
Lesson seven. Reading the weights. Because the pilot is linear, we can understand exactly what it learned. Let's take it apart.

Start with one decision. The lander is high up and falling fast. Each input is multiplied by its weight, and the products are added up per action. The falling speed gives the main engine a big push, and takes a lot away from do nothing. It's close, but the main engine wins. A moment later, the lander is tilted to the right. The tilt now adds votes to the left engine and takes them from the others. The left engine wins, and turns the lander back upright. Further down, the lander is spinning to the left. Spin has the biggest weight of all, on the right engine, and here it counts for it. The right engine wins, and spins the lander back. And on the ground, with both legs down. The two leg switches each add a big vote for do nothing. Do nothing wins, and the lander stays still. That's the rule the settle penalty taught it.

But be careful. A big weight doesn't always mean a big effect. Here are the sizes of all the weights. What also matters is how much each input actually changes in flight. Altitude and drift move a lot. Spin moves less, so its large weights are multiplied by smaller numbers. The legs are always zero in the air. Multiply the two, and you get the influence of each weight. The ones that matter most are tilt and spin on the right engine, and drift on the left engine.

We can also draw a rule as a map. Across is the tilt, and up and down is the spin, with every other input held at a typical value. Each colour is the action the pilot would choose there. The white line is a real flight. The border between the two engines runs diagonally through the middle. Tilt or spin one way, and the pilot fires the engine that turns it back, so it stays upright with small corrections.

Here's a second map. Across is the height, and up and down is the falling speed. Falling fast and low, it fires the main engine. Falling slowly, it steers with the side engines instead. And high up, it doesn't brake yet. It saves the main engine for later. The real flight rides along that border all the way down.

Now let's put it together, one action at a time. The main engine is the brake. Falling speed has the biggest weight on it, so the faster the lander falls, the harder it wants to brake. Do nothing is the landing rule. Each leg that touches the ground adds a big vote for it. With both legs down, it wins, and the engines go quiet. The left engine fixes drift and tilt. It fires when the lander drifts right, sits right of the pad, tilts right, or spins clockwise. It pushes the lander back toward the middle. And the right engine is its mirror image. Drifting left, tilting left, or spinning the other way, and the right engine pushes back. Nobody told evolution the lander is symmetric. It found that on its own.

Finally, let's test which weights the pilot really needs. We set one weight to zero, fly thirty episodes, and see how many still land. Then we put it back, and try the next one. Most weights can go with little harm. But remove the rule that links falling speed to the main engine, and not a single flight lands. Without it, the pilot never brakes, and simply falls. The leg rules matter almost as much. Remove one of them, and most landings fail.
